newsitem.title: UK: Summary of latest opinion polls on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Summary of latest opinion polls on EMU.

text.p: The following is a summary of findings from recent opinion polls about European economic and monetary union (EMU).

SWEDEN, May 6 - Opposition to joining monetary union is falling, with every second Swede now supporting participation, according to a poll comissioned by JP Bank and daily Finanstidningen and carried out by pollster Sifo. The number of Swedes opposing EMU fell to 35 percent in May from 37 percent in an earlier poll in March. Of the 50 percent in favour of membership, 26 percent want Sweden to join from the start in 1999, up from 24 percent in March, while 24 percent want to wait, unchanged from the previous month. Fifteen percent were undecided in the May poll.

AUSTRIA, April 28 - Austrian dissatisfaction with the European Union is running at an all-time high at 64 percent, a survey showed on Monday, and only 34 percent of those polled saw more advantages from EU membership. Asked how they would vote were there a vote next Sunday, 62 percent of those polled said they would oppose EU membership while 36 percent would vote in favour, the survey conducted by the Austrian research institute Market said.

SWEDEN, April 25 - Most local activists of Sweden's minority ruling Social Democrats want Sweden to stay outside Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) at its 1999 start to be able to see how it works, Dagens Industri newspaper said on Friday. A survey by the newspaper showed that 178 local Social Democratic representatives out of a total 350 thought Sweden should wait and see and possibly join EMU at a later stage.

FINLAND, April 24 - Eighty-four percent of Finnish companies want Finland to join the European economic and monetary union (EMU) quickly among the first countries, two leading industry lobbies said on Thursday. "As much as 84 percent (in a recent poll) favoured joining quickly, along with the first countries, 14 percent wanted a slower timetable and the rest said Finland should not join at all," the Confederation of Industry and Employers (TT) and the Central Chamber of Commerce (CCC) said in a joint statement. Ten percent wanted Finland to wait for Sweden's decision, they said.

BRITAIN, April 17 - A MORI poll for the Times newspaper showed nearly three-fifths of the public endorse Prime Minister John Major's line that Britain should keep its options open on a single currency.

EUROPE, April 17 - Chances of European currency union starting on time seem to be improving because fewer countries are expected to qualify from the outset, EMU analysts said in a Reuters survey. All respondents were 100 percent sure that France, Germany and the Netherlands would be in the first wave. Austria, Belgium and Luxembourg were rated 100 percent certainties by 82 percent, 84 percent and 97 percent of respondents respectively. The poll also showed that the Maastricht criteria would not necessarily guarantee convergence in the continent's economies.
GERMANY, April 7 - Most German voters want the single currency to be delayed but a majority do not want the euro to be a campaign issue in next year's election, an Emnid poll showed.

FINLAND, April 3 - A survey among slightly more than 2,000 people by polling institute Taloustutkimus Oy found opposition to EMU rising to 46 percent in February/March from 41 percent in February, and support fell to 36 percent from 38 percent. The rest were undecided.

SWEDEN, April 1 - Only 19 percent of Swedes want Sweden to be in the first wave of countries to join EMU, according to a survey by pollster Skop. Almost a quarter of the 1,000 people questioned gave a flat no to EMU membership, according to the poll published by tabloid paper Aftonbladet.

EUROPE, March 27 - Market expectations of a broad-based start to EMU in 1999 edged lower, with the perceived probability of Italy taking part dipping below 50 percent, according to the JP Morgan "EMU calculator".

FRANCE, March 25 - A BVA survey for French radio BFM found that 64 percent of French adults believed both that France would be among those joining EMU from 1999 and that it was necessary that it do so.

SWEDEN, March 25 - Sixty-eight percent of Swedish market players expected EMU to start as planned in 1999, according to a March survey by pollster TEMO, compared with 80 percent in February. The poll also showed that seven percent of market players believed Sweden would join EMU from the start, down from 10 percent in February's survey.

GERMANY, March 20 - A survey by Manager magazine found that over four-fifths of 100 German executives questioned expected the launch of EMU to go ahead as planned. It also found that many companies planned to switch to euros as a means of payment before euro notes and coins are issued in 2002.

DENMARK, March 17 - A Gallup poll published in the Berlingske Tidende showed 41 percent of respondents believed Denmark should reverse its 1993 decision not to join EMU, compared with 46 percent in December. The survey, carried out between March 12 and 14, showed 49 percent in favour of maintaining the Danish 'no' to a common European currency, compared with 44 percent in December.

GERMANY, March 15 - The Infratest Burke financial research institute said only 37 percent of Germans accepted planned currency union, while 57 percent were against it, the Welt am Sonntag newspaper reported. The poll, of 700 residents of the former West Germany with a monthly income of at least 5,000 marks, showed seven out of every 10 thought EMU, due to start in 1999, would happen, though only 40 percent thought Germany would fulfil the conditions laid out in the Maastricht treaty.

GERMANY, March 13 - Three-quarters of German voters think Europe's planned single currency should be delayed if member countries do not meet the Maastricht criteria. The Forsa survey in the weekly Die Woche said a mere 14 percent argued for softening the tough line backed by the Bundesbank and Finance Minister Theo Waigel in order to allow the launch to take place on schedule in 1999. Die Woche also published two bank surveys showing widespread scepticism among business executives about the monetary union. Only 22 percent were positive about it and only 14 percent expected it to start on time.

BRITAIN, March 10 - Almost two-thirds of UK fund managers said EMU would significantly change their investment plans, but almost an equal number expect the start date for the single currency to be postponed, a monthly Gallup poll of fund managers showed. A majority of continental European fund managers believe EMU will take place on time and only a third said it would change their investment plans.

GERMANY, March 6 - More than half of German voters want the strict economic criteria to qualify for Europe's planned single currency to be softened and only one-fifth think they should be applied strictly, according to a survey by the respected Allensbach Institute. The poll also said 47.6 percent of the sample group opposed the euro, while 41.6 percent said they supported it. Only 10.8 percent were undecided. On the criteria, 55.2 percent said they should be softened, while 19.6 percent wanted to see them applied as laid down in the Maastricht Treaty, according to the poll.

AUSTRIA, March 5 - Nearly 50 percent of Austrians believe conversion to a European single currency, scheduled for 1999, will make their savings less valuable, a survey by market research institute Spectra showed. Nearly 40 percent expected the euro to be a disadvantage for Austria. Only 15 percent thought it would bring benefits.

FINLAND, March 3 - A Reuters poll found 22 of 23 dealers, analysts and economists surveyed at banks and corporate treasury departments believed Finland would be in the first group of countries to join stage three of EMU, if it started on time in 1999.

BRITAIN, Feb 27 - The UK retail banking sector is significantly behind its continental European competitors in preparations for introduction of the euro, Coopers & Lybrand said in a survey. The survey found continental Europeans did not see UK banks as a threat "largely because they do not believe that the UK will join the EMU at its outset."
-- London Polling Unit +44 171 542 5223
